question: The total resistance of 10 resistors of equal resistance R arranged in series arrangement is _____.
solution:
The correct answer is __**10R**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• When resistors are arranged in a **series connection**, the total resistance is the **sum of the individual resistances**. This means all resistances are added together without any modification.
 
• The formula for total resistance in a series connection is **Rₜₒₜₐₗ = R₁ + R₂ + ... + Rₙ**, where Rₙ is the resistance of each resistor.
 
• In the given problem, there are **10 resistors** of equal resistance, each having a resistance value of **R**.
 
• Applying the series formula: **Rₜₒₜₐₗ = R + R + R + ... (10 times)**. Therefore, **Rₜₒₜₐₗ = 10R**.
 
• **Option 2** is the correct answer because the total resistance of 10 resistors in series is 10R, as derived from the above calculation.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Series Combination of Resistors:**

 
 
• In a series connection, the current flowing through all the resistors remains the **same**, but the voltage across each resistor may vary depending on its resistance.
 
• The total resistance in series is always **greater** than the largest individual resistance in the circuit.
 
• Example: If three resistors of 2Ω, 4Ω, and 6Ω are connected in series, the total resistance will be **2 + 4 + 6 = 12Ω**.
 
 
 
• **Parallel Combination of Resistors:**
 
 
• In a parallel connection, the total resistance is calculated using the formula: **1/Rₜₒₜₐₗ = 1/R₁ + 1/R₂ + ... + 1/Rₙ**.
 
• The total resistance in a parallel circuit is always **less** than the smallest individual resistance.
 
• Example: If two resistors of 4Ω and 6Ω are connected in parallel, the total resistance is calculated as **1/Rₜₒₜₐₗ = 1/4 + 1/6 = 5/12; Rₜₒₜₐₗ = 12/5 = 2.4Ω**.
 
 
 
• **Applications of Series and Parallel Circuits:**
 
 
• **Series circuits** are commonly used in devices like **string lights** or older Christmas lights, where all lights will go off if one fails.
 
• **Parallel circuits** are widely used in **household wiring** to ensure that the failure of one appliance does not affect others.
 
 
 
• **Key Differences Between Series and Parallel Circuits:**
 
 
• In a series circuit, the current is the same across all components, while in a parallel circuit, the voltage is the same across all components.
 
• Series circuits are not suitable for high-power applications due to high resistance, whereas parallel circuits are more efficient for such cases.
